description: The pinned line-item money keys (Section 7.2). A line item states its money as integer minor units under unit_price_minor and total_minor; the bare names unit_price and total are refused rather than read as major units. Both reference implementations decide accept/reject from this file, and the Python suite also validates every line-item case against spec/schemas/offer.schema.json, so the schema and the two implementations cannot drift apart. A few cases JSON cannot express — NaN, Infinity — are asserted inline in each language's suite instead, and say so there.
integral_value_rule: A pinned amount is an integer VALUE, not a particular JSON spelling. RFC 8785 makes 36000 and 36000.0 the same number, and JavaScript cannot tell them apart once parsed, so an integral number is accepted however it was written — 36000, 36000.0, 3.6e4 — and -0.0 normalises to 0. A number with a fractional part is refused, and so are NaN, Infinity, strings, and booleans, which are not numbers at all. The magnitude bound is JavaScript's safe-integer range, 9007199254740991: past it a double can no longer represent adjacent integers distinctly, so the two implementations could read one JSON document as two different amounts. Bounding makes them agree exactly, and no real line states 90 trillion currency units.

minor_unit_conversion_rule: sign(v) * floor(abs(v) * 100 + 0.5): scale by the currency exponent, then round half AWAY FROM ZERO. Python's math.floor and TypeScript's Math.floor over the same operations in the same order agree bit for bit; every case below was measured in both. Rounding away from zero rather than up is what lets a debit and the credit that offsets it cancel: under half-up, 2.675 and -2.675 converted to 268 and -267, leaving a minor unit behind on every offsetting pair. A vendor amount is a decimal figure, not a numeric literal: a string is accepted only as optional sign, ASCII digits and at most one decimal point, after stripping ASCII space, tab, newline and carriage return. Hex, octal, binary, underscore separators, exponent notation, non-ASCII digits, 'NaN' and 'Infinity' are refused rather than left to each language's parser, which reads several of them differently. A money object contributes its amount member, or its value member when amount is absent OR null, because a present-but-null member states no amount. The result is bounded by the safe-integer range. Rounding to nearest does not make the conversion exact: exactness needs the source as a decimal STRING, because once a float exists the decimal the vendor wrote is already gone. That is a separate change from this one.
